title: Checkpoint: Foundations
subtitle: Apply networking, HTTP, API, latency, and state concepts without lesson-level cues
objectives: Recall foundations cold, without the cue of knowing which unit a question came from
Connect ideas across units: physics, protocols, contracts, and state
Diagnose a scenario that spans several units at once

exercises.prompt: Two stateless servers have enough capacity, but clients connect directly to one address. Put a load balancer in front so either server can answer.
exercises.beforeStatus: SERVER A · overloaded · Server B · idle
exercises.afterStatus: SERVER A · half traffic · Server B · half traffic
exercises.why: Stateless request handling lets the load balancer send a request to either server because required durable state is not trapped in one server's memory.

exercises.prompt: Draw the failure path first; the disconnected or blocked part is evidence: Two stateless servers have enough capacity, but clients connect directly to one address. Put a load balancer in front so either server can answer.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Clients → Server A. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Stateless request handling lets the load balancer send a request to either server because required durable state is not trapped in one server's memory.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: Two stateless servers have enough capacity, but clients connect directly to one address. Put a load balancer in front so either server can answer. Place Load balancer, Server A, Server B. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Clients → Load balancer; Load balancer → Server A; Load balancer → Server B. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Stateless request handling lets the load balancer send a request to either server because required durable state is not trapped in one server's memory.

exercises.prompt: Your API server responds in 3ms. A user in Sydney says the app is slow. Your servers are in Virginia. What's the dominant cost?
choices: The network round trip — physics puts a floor under Virginia↔Sydney that no server speed can beat
exercises.why: The server contributes 3ms, while the Virginia–Sydney network round trip is roughly 200ms. Propagation distance therefore dominates the response time; moving computation closer to the user or reducing round trips can help, while optimizing a few milliseconds of server work cannot remove the network floor.

exercises.prompt: Order the main steps after you enter `https://api.example.com/users/42` in a fresh browser.
steps: Domain Name System (DNS) resolves `api.example.com` to an IP address
The client opens a transport connection to that address
Transport Layer Security (TLS) authenticates the server and establishes encryption
The client sends an HTTP `GET /users/42` request
The server returns an HTTP response with status, headers, and a body
exercises.why: Name resolution supplies an address before the client can connect. Transport Layer Security (TLS) then establishes the protected channel used by HTTPS, and HTTP carries the application request and response over that channel. Cached DNS or reused connections can skip work on later requests, but this is the dependency order for a fresh path.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are STATE — things the system must remember? Select all.
choices: A pure function that formats a date
A Domain Name System (DNS) resolver's cached record and expiry time
exercises.why: A session, an uploaded file, and a cached Domain Name System (DNS) record plus its expiry all influence later requests, so each is state. The date formatter retains no information between calls; the same input alone determines its output. Cached state remains state even when it is disposable and time-bounded.

exercises.prompt: Your API receives malformed JSON and cannot process the request. Which response best matches the failure?
exercises.why: `400 Bad Request` tells the client that the request syntax or representation is invalid, so retrying the same bytes will not help. `500 Internal Server Error` describes an unexpected server failure, `503 Service Unavailable` a temporary inability to serve, and `403 Forbidden` a refusal to authorize an understood request.

exercises.prompt: Match each foundation to the unit idea it belongs to.

pairs.right: Turns a name into an IP address
Any healthy equivalent server can handle the next request using shared state
A contract-bound operation exposed at a method and path
A threshold at or below which 99% of observations fall

exercises.why: Domain Name System (DNS) resolution maps a domain name to records such as IP addresses. Stateless servers keep session state outside one process, so any healthy server can handle the next request. An API endpoint combines a method and path with a request/response contract, and p99 latency is the threshold at or below which 99% of observations fall.

exercises.prompt: Which statements match HTTP method semantics? Select all.
choices: `GET` is safe and idempotent: the requested operation should not change server state
`PUT` is idempotent but not safe: repeating the same full replacement has the same intended effect
`DELETE` is idempotent even if a repeated call returns a different status after the resource is gone
HTTP requires every `POST` to create a new resource on every execution
exercises.why: HTTP defines safe methods as read-only in their requested semantics and idempotent methods by the intended effect of repeated identical requests. `GET` is both; `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent but mutate state. `POST` has no general idempotency guarantee, yet an endpoint can make a particular POST retry-safe through its own contract, such as a client-supplied deduplication key.

exercises.prompt: Place the profile authority and its two read copies: writes land once, then copies update from that source.
exercises.why: The write API commits the authoritative database row; replication and cache population derive read copies from it. Either copy can lag, so reads need a freshness policy and sensitive read-after-write paths may need the primary; treating a cache or replica as an independent authority can resurrect stale profile data after updates.

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: Place the profile authority and its two read copies: writes land once, then copies update from that source.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Profile Write API → Primary Database Row; Primary Database Row → Read Replica; Primary Database Row → Profile Cache. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The write API commits the authoritative database row; replication and cache population derive read copies from it. Either copy can lag, so reads need a freshness policy and sensitive read-after-write paths may need the primary; treating a cache or replica as an independent authority can resurrect stale profile data after updates.

exercises.prompt: You cache a user's profile for 60 seconds. What have you actually bought and sold?
choices: Bought speed and reduced load; sold freshness — for up to 60 seconds a reader can see the past
exercises.why: A 60-second time to live (TTL) lets the cache serve the stored profile until that entry expires. Reads become faster and avoid database work, while a database update can remain invisible through this cache for up to 60 seconds unless the entry is explicitly invalidated. The TTL is acceptable only when that staleness window fits the product's correctness requirement.

exercises.prompt: Every request flows left to right. Each component's capacity is shown. Tap the one that limits the whole system.
exercises.why: Every request must pass through the app-server stage, whose 6,000 requests/second capacity is the smallest in the path. The end-to-end throughput therefore cannot exceed 6,000 requests/second. Increasing cache capacity would leave this ceiling unchanged until app-server capacity also increases or work is removed from that stage.

exercises.prompt: Your app has 10,000 requests/second and a 99.9% success rate. How worried should you be?
choices: That's 10 failures every second, roughly 864,000 a day — convert percentages to rates before deciding they're fine
exercises.why: A 99.9% success rate leaves a 0.1% failure rate. Applied to 10,000 requests/second, that is 10 failed requests each second, or about 864,000 per day if the rate is sustained. Whether that is acceptable depends on the affected operation, but the absolute failure volume is large enough to require investigation.

exercises.prompt: A teammate wants to store the shopping cart in server memory 'because it's fastest.' What's the one question that settles it?
choices: How much memory do we have?
If this server died right now, what would we lose — and who else needs to read this?
exercises.why: A cart stored only in one server's memory disappears when that process restarts and is unavailable when another server handles the user. Because the cart must survive server failure and be shared across devices or application instances, it belongs in durable shared storage; local memory may still hold a disposable cache copy.

exercises.prompt: What connects DNS caching, a CDN, a read replica, and a browser cache?
choices: They're all copies kept near the reader — each buys speed and each can be stale
exercises.why: DNS caches, content delivery network edges, read replicas, and browser caches all serve derived data from a location closer to the reader or with cheaper access. They reduce latency or source load while introducing a period in which a reader may observe an older value. Their refresh and invalidation policies should match the cost of that staleness.

exercises.prompt: A smart thermostat resolves a service name, opens HTTPS, sends a reading, and receives `503`. Which conclusions are supported?
choices: The thermostat never opened a connection
Routing and HTTP reached a server, but that server could not currently handle the request
exercises.why: An HTTP response proves the request reached an HTTP-speaking endpoint. `503 Service Unavailable` reports temporary inability to serve; it does not imply DNS or connection setup failed.
